paragraphs.text: Huiliu means [returned](malaysian-returned-liu-bao:returned), and on this label Malaysia names a stop in the life of the tea, not where it grew. This [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) was made in Guangxi in the 1990s. The shop traces it from Guangzhou to storage in Malaysia and Singapore, then back to Guangzhou again.

That journey follows an old road. A [trade account published in 1951](malaysian-returned-liu-bao:river-trade) follows Liu Bao downstream, changing to a larger wooden boat at Libu for Fengkai and then to a powered vessel for Guangzhou, with Ipoh and Kuala Lumpur among its final markets. The tea was made for [Chinese miners and labourers in Malaya](liu-bao:nanyang-trade), above all in the tin mines. Older tea has since been [finding its way back](malaysian-returned-liu-bao:tea-came-back): on a visit to Wuzhou in 2024, the Malaysian trade representative Lin Hengyi saw a 1973 import order linking a Malaysian firm with a Wuzhou tea company, and merchants there asked him about bringing older Liu Bao back to the Chinese market.

At thirty-one years this lot is well past the ten after which the trade counts a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged). Its years abroad are part of that count, because how the tea was stored matters as much as how long, and the [place a lot was kept](liu-bao:old-stock) gives it its own character.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
